svg.aria-label: Diagram: the Google Cloud IAM principal types and their identifier prefixes, why only groups scale, the two limits on an allow policy that pull in opposite directions, and the audit logging exemptions that share the principal budget
svg.title: IAM principals: six kinds, two limits that fight each other, and why only groups scale
svg.text: The role decides what can be done. The principal decides how long that stays correct.
A perfectly scoped role granted to a named person is wrong the day they change team, and goes on being wrong quietly.
Six kinds of principal, and the prefix tells you which — several are not people
user:
One human. Break-glass and singular ownership — not routine access.
group:
A Google group, by membership. Everything routine. The default.
serviceAccount:
A workload identity — and also a resource, with a policy of its own.
domain:
Every identity in a domain. A company-wide grant in the syntax of one user.
principalSet:
A pool, or all service accounts in a project, folder, or organization.
allUsers · allAuthenticatedUsers
Anyone on the internet. Deliberate, or an incident.
Only one of them has a population that changes without touching a policy
Someone joins or leaves, and if they were bound as
user:
every allow policy they appear in has to change, found by searching the estate
group:
one membership list changes, outside IAM entirely
domain:
nothing changes — which is the problem, not the feature
1,500 principals per allow policy
IAM does not deduplicate principals that appear in
more than one role binding.
So it is a budget on bindings × principals, not on
people. This limit punishes granting to individuals.
250 domains and groups per allow policy
Every distinct group you invent counts toward it.
So this limit punishes solving the first one by
inventing a group per team per role.
The two limits pull in opposite directions.
Between them they describe the shape of the answer
Four roles for 400 people is 1,600 principals and fails. Four roles for four groups is 16, whatever they contain.
A modest number of durable groups, bound a few times, with the churn absorbed by membership.
And the budget is shared with something that is not access control
The 1,500 counts appearances in role bindings AND the principals the policy exempts from Data Access audit logging.
Nothing about a logging exemption suggests it will exhaust an allow policy. Check the count before adding them.
The strongest quantitative argument for groups in the whole of IAM is on a quotas page, not in the guidance.
